messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Re: Re[2]: [stan-users] question: can actual data be outside 95%CI of replicated data
parts:
Usually when you define 95% intervals you're saying that something has a 95% chance of being in that interval. That means 5% of the time you're outside of it.

Your data being outside the 95% intervals of your posterior predictives can also mean that your model isn't doing a good job of explaining your data.

Is it 5% of your data that's outside of the 95% intervals? (this is perfectly normal)

Or is most of your data outside of the intervals? (this can easily happen when you're modeling, and usually means you need to change your model)

Ben

messages.author: 484c91357ac83f6b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] question: can actual data be outside 95%CI of replicated data
parts:
In average, 5% of data will be outside of a 95% "CI" obtained directly the true data generating function itself (that is, an interval with 95% probability that a new data point will be inside the interval, given the true data generating function).

So an interval with estimated probability of 95% shouldn't be any better and in fact, if it is "better" than that, then it might be a bad feature... just imagine: you could just say that your CI is the whole line of real numbers (or whatever sample space you have), then your data would be 100% there (and that's why any sensible loss functions would penalize the "size" of the interval since otherwise, you could just choose the full sample space and forget statistics).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] question: can actual data be outside 95%CI of replicated data
parts:
> On May 13, 2017, at 7:59 PM, Ben B <bbba...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Usually when you define 95% intervals you're saying that something has a 95% chance of being in that interval. That means 5% of the time you're outside of it.
>
> Your data being outside the 95% intervals of your posterior predictives can also mean that your model isn't doing a good job of explaining your data.

It depends on what we're talking about here. This can happen even
when you're using exactly the same model as was used to generate
the data. In fact, it'll happen 5% of the time. In that case, it's
a "bad" draw of data.

This can also happen if the model's misspecified, which is usually
why we run these on real data.

- Bob
